rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's recitation says that worldly life is all there is: people die and live.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: In a divine report, God says that people harm Him by cursing time; He is time, holds command, and turns night and day.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses al-dahr as time.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A divine report forbids saying that time has brought disappointment: God sends night and day and can seize them when He wills.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Another divine report says God lent to a servant who did not repay, and the servant abused Him by saying alas, time, though God is time.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمر
rows.claim: Ibn Umar rebukes a man who tried to take his cloak, reminding onlookers that death, the grave, the two interrogating angels, and resurrection precede the loss of falsifiers.
rows.anchor: فقال يا أخي: أما علمت أن الموت أمامك

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says each community will be distinct when brought to account.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains that the communities will be made to kneel on their knees.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says they will be on their knees at the reckoning.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Aisha reports the Prophet's endurance of fasting and hardship: God required the resolute messengers and Muhammad to bear what they disliked and forgo what they loved.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the resolute messengers as Muhammad, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus.

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliyah lists Noah, Hud, and Abraham, with Muhammad as the fourth; their examples show them openly separating from their people's polytheism.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada lists Noah, Hud, Abraham, Shuayb, and Moses as the resolute messengers.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن عساكر عن قتادة في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj lists Ishmael, Jacob, and Job as resolute, while excluding Adam, Jonah, and Solomon.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن المنذر عن ابن جريج

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the resolute messengers were those commanded to fight until they had carried it through: Noah, Hud, Salih, Moses, David, and Solomon.

rows.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Jabir reports that the resolute messengers numbered 313.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says only a culpable unbeliever is destroyed: either a polytheist who turns his back on Islam or a hypocrite whose heart contradicts his profession.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Anas transmits a prayer for success that invokes God's mercy, forgiveness, safety, good deeds, Paradise, and deliverance from Hell, and includes the two verses about the briefness of worldly time.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses lughub as toil or fatigue.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله {وما مسنا من لغوب} قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rejects the Jewish claim that God became fatigued after creating the heavens and earth.

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز
rows.claim: Abu Majliz says sitting with one leg over the other is permissible; Jews disliked the posture because they claimed God rested after creation on the Sabbath.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet identifies glorification before sunrise with the dawn prayer and before sunset with the afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: عن جرير بن عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd interprets glorification at night as the evening prayer and after prostrations as voluntary prayers.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes glorification at night to mean the whole night.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the two units before dawn and two after sunset are called the after-stars and after-prostrations prayers.

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali reports the Prophet's same identification: two units after sunset are after-prostrations and two before dawn are after-stars.

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra says the ten voluntary units he learned from the Prophet include the two units after sunset named in this verse.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid gives an interpretation rendered in the source as al-jimāʿ, a gathering or conjunction.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also interprets the locations as the stars of the sky.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the oath is by the places where stars set or fall.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan interprets the stars' locations as their scattering and falling apart on the Resurrection Day.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan also glosses the locations as where stars disappear.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets the locations as the stars' stations or courses.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies both the star locations and the tremendous oath as the Quran.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran descended all at once on Laylat al-Qadr from the highest heaven to the lowest, then came down over the years in installments.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas associates the sites with the Quran's successive stars of revelation.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran descended to the lowest heaven together, then reached earth in groups of three, five, or varying numbers of verses.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's reading takes the oath as by the decisive parts of the Quran sent down successively.
rows.anchor: عن المنهال بن عمرو رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets the stars' locations as the decisive Quran.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the sites are the repository of the Book, from its beginning to its end.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabi says the Quran is in the hidden Book, the Preserved Tablet, and the purified ones who touch it are angels purified of sins.
rows.anchor: عن الربيع بن أنس رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the Quran is in its hidden book, untouched by dust, and only angels touch it.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies the hidden Book with the Torah and Gospel and the purified ones with their bearers.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reports that Ibn Masud read the phrase with a declarative mā: no one touches it except the purified.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the heavenly revealed Book is touched only by angels.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas identifies the purified ones as angels.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada distinguishes the heavenly text, touched only by angels, from earthly copies that polytheists, impure people, and hypocrites may touch.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report attributed to the Prophet says the Quran is with God in purified sheets, touched by those brought near.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud applies Satan's promise to the disbelievers and hypocrites who lived in the Prophet's time.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the person whom Satan tells to disbelieve means people generally.

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-A'mash recited the consequence as both Satan and the person remaining forever in Hell.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: After seeing needy people from Mudar, the Prophet recited the warning to remember tomorrow, urged charity before it became impossible, and taught that whoever starts a good or bad practice shares its reward or burden; the community gave and he distributed it.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says what a person sends ahead for tomorrow means the Day of Resurrection.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {ما قدمت لغد}

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr's sermon warns that lifespans are hidden and urges people to remain wary, recalling that those who forget God are made to forget themselves.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr asks where former companions and tyrants have gone, and urges listeners to use the Quran's light and counsel for the coming darkness.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr cites the Quran's praise of people who hastened to good works and called upon God in hope and fear.

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr says speech without God's pleasure, wealth not spent in God's path, anger that defeats forbearance, and fear of blame in God's cause bring no good.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says that if the Quran were sent upon a mountain with the commands and warnings given to people, it would split and humble itself; people are more obliged to fear and soften their hearts.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك في قوله: {لو أنزلنا هذا القرآن على جبل}

rows.speaker: مالك بن دينار
rows.claim: Malik ibn Dinar swears that no servant truly believes this Quran without the heart splitting.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Quran's weight and fear would make a mountain split and humble; people should receive it with intense fear and humility so they may reflect.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says righteous members of his community are not distracted by trade or sale from remembering God and performing the five obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says a person able to perform pilgrimage or owing zakat who neglects it will ask to return at death; Ibn Abbas supports the warning by reciting the whole surah.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a dying believer who withheld zakat, pilgrimage dues, or another due to God will ask to return and give charity and zakat; God will not delay the appointed term.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says remembrance means the five prayers, while spending from one's provision means zakat and expenditure for pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك في قوله: {لا تلهكم أموالكم ولا أولادكم عن ذكر الله}

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata identifies remembrance of God here with the obligatory prayer.
rows.anchor: عن عطاء في قوله: {لا تلهكم أموالكم ولا أولادكم عن ذكر الله}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses fa-aṣṣaddaq as paying zakat and being among the righteous as performing pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: الحسن عن عاصم
rows.claim: Al-Hasan reports Asim's recitation of wa-aku and interprets the requested righteous deed as pilgrimage.

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Thabit says Quranic reading is a transmitted Sunnah, so people should recite as taught; he cites the readings in Ta-Ha and this verse.

rows.speaker: الحسن ومحمد
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Muhammad say a woman's waiting period ends if she miscarries.

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Sha'bi says a formed fetus that miscarries in the fourth stage frees an enslaved mother and ends her waiting period.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas forbids intercourse with a purchased pregnant slave woman until she delivers, citing the term for pregnant divorcees.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says a divorced woman must be housed according to one's means, even if only a corner of the home is available.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة {أسكنوهن من حيث سكنتم من وجدكم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses min wajdikum as according to your means.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also defines wajd as means and says the prohibition on harming divorced women refers to constricting their housing.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله: {من حيث سكنتم من وجدكم}

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim recited wajd with a ḍamma on the wāw.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a pregnant divorcee receives housing and maintenance until delivery, then nursing support until weaning; an irrevocably divorced nonpregnant woman receives housing through her waiting period but no maintenance.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله: {وإن كن أولات حمل فأنفقوا عليهن حتى يضعن حملهن}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says a mother has the stronger claim to nurse her child at the rate the father would have paid another nurse.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr interprets disagreement over nursing as a case where another wet nurse is hired; he also says that once a wage is set, the mother may choose.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير {وإن تعاسرتم فسترضع له أخرى}

rows.speaker: إبراهيم والضحاك وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibrahim, al-Dahhak, and Qatada transmit the same interpretation about disagreement over breastfeeding.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid applies spending according to means to a divorced woman who nurses for the father.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله: {لينفق ذو سعة من سعته ومن قدر عليه رزقه فلينفق مما آتاه الله}

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj glosses constrained provision as restricted, and what God has given as what He granted.

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar sent Abu Ubayda money after learning he dressed and ate austerely; when Abu Ubayda used it for comfort, Umar said he had applied the command to spend according to one's means.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A weak report says a believer taught by God spends generously when given abundance and restricts spending when provision is restricted.
rows.anchor: عن طاووس قال: قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says three donors who each gave one tenth of their wealth receive equal reward, whatever the size of their wealth.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Malik al-Ashari transmits the same teaching: donors of one tenth of their differing fortunes are equal in reward.

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhri says an unable husband should be given time rather than separated from his wife, citing that God burdens each only within what He granted; Ma'mar says Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz agreed.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the severe accounting as showing no mercy and the strange punishment as great and terrible.

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim recited nukran with a doubled consonant.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the mark on the snout is a sign that will never leave him.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {سنسمه على الخرطوم}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada's second wording says the mark remains with the person to the end.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {سنسمه على الخرطوم}

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: Asim read the phrase with two hamzas as an interrogative.
rows.anchor: عن عاصم أنه قرأ {أن كان ذا مال وبنين}

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says a person who dies slandering, mocking, and nicknaming people will be marked by God on both sides of the snout at resurrection.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says these are people whose story God has recounted and made clear.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {إنا بلوناهم كما بلونا أصحاب الجنة}

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports that Abu Jahl ordered the captives at Badr bound in the mountains rather than killed; the verse likens his power over them to the garden owners' power over their orchard.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the owners of the garden as People of the Book.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they were people of Abyssinia whose father fed the needy from his garden; after his death, his sons swore to harvest early and give no poor person food.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the garden belonged to an Israelite elder who saved his annual provisions and gave away the excess; his sons opposed charity and resolved to exclude the needy.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr locates the garden in a place in Yemen called Dar, six miles from Sana'a.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير في قوله

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says their exception was the phrase Subhan Allah.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the visitor that passed over the garden as a command from God.

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj identifies the visitor as a punishment, a fiery mass from a valley of Hell.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God's command came upon the garden at night while its owners slept, leaving it like the dark night; Qatr ibn Maymun agrees.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {فطاف عليها طائف من ربك وهم نائمون}

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet warns that sin can cause lost knowledge, missed night prayer, and withheld provision, then says the owners lost their garden because of their sin.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: إياكم والمعاصي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses al-sarim as the black night.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In a dialogue with Nafi ibn al-Azraq, Ibn Abbas says al-sarim means gold and cites an anonymous poem using the word al-sarim.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says their cultivated plot was a vineyard.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله: أن {اغدوا على حرثكم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they were whispering and speaking quietly.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they whispered their plan to exclude the poor; they went early, resolved and thinking themselves able to carry it out.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the owners as having power or ability.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says they went out intent on a plan they had settled among themselves: no poor person would enter.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد قال: {وغدوا على حرد قادرين}

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima glosses hard as anger.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة في قوله: {وغدوا على حرد}

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says they were resolutely set against the poor.
rows.anchor: عن الحسن في قوله: {وغدوا على حرد}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says they first thought they had lost the way to their garden.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they first thought they had taken the wrong road, then recognized the garden and realized they had been deprived.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada calls the middle brother the most just and best in alarm and in returning to the right course.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {إنا لضالون} قال: أخطأنا الطريق ما هذه جنتنا وفي قوله: {بل نحن محرومون}

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says after recognizing the garden's landmarks, they called themselves deprived and afflicted by misfortune.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Asked whether the garden owners were people of Paradise or Hell, Qatada says the question burdened him and gives no answer.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses awsaṭuhum as the fairest or most just of them.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد عن مجاهد في وقوله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says awsaṭ means most just wherever it occurs in the Quran.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also glosses awsaṭuhum as the most just.

rows.speaker: السري
rows.claim: Al-Sari says their way of making an exception in that era was glorification.
rows.anchor: عن السري في قوله: {ألم أقل لكم لولا تسبحون}

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says they should have said an exception when swearing to harvest early; their tasbih served as their equivalent of saying God willing.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets the present punishment as worldly punishment and the hereafter's punishment as the punishment of the next life.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses the question about who will guarantee the claim as asking who is its guarantor.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {كذلك العذاب} قال: عقوبة الدنيا {ولعذاب الآخرة} قال: عقوبة الآخرة وفي قوله: {سلهم أيهم بذلك زعيم}

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says tadrusuna means you read, and the oath binding upon Us means a binding covenant.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas calls haluʿ impatient and easily distressed, says it was revealed about Abu Jahl, and cites Bashr ibn Abi Hazim's poetry for the word's Arabic usage.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains the created disposition by reading the next verses: a person despairs in adversity and withholds in prosperity.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr glosses haluʿ as miserly and easily distressed.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير في قوله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says haluʿ means fretful.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses haluʿ as given to anguish.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses haluʿ as greedy.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: حصين بن عبد الرحمن
rows.claim: Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman glosses haluʿ as avid or grasping.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak describes haluʿ as someone never satisfied with gathering wealth.

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report attributed to Ali says a sick person's groaning is recorded: a patient person earns good deeds, while one who despairs is recorded as haluʿ and receives no reward.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Daniel described Muhammad's community as praying in a way that would have saved earlier peoples from their disasters; prayer is a fine believer's trait.

rows.speaker: إبراهيم التيمي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Taymi says those constant in prayer maintain the obligatory prayers.
rows.anchor: عن إبراهيم التيمي رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says constancy in prayer means keeping its appointed times; Masruq reports the same.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين
rows.claim: Imran ibn Husayn says the constant worshipper does not look around during prayer.
rows.anchor: عن عمران بن حصين رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: حضرمى
rows.claim: Al-Hadrami reports that a prominent jinn offered to protect Muhammad, claiming he would shelter him, and the verse was revealed in response.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Masud recounts that the jinn chief Wardan offered to keep the jinn away from the Prophet, who replied that none could protect him from God.

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses multahad as refuge.
rows.anchor: عن الضحاك في قوله: {ولن أجد من دونه ملتحدا}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the Prophet has no refuge or helper except conveying God's messages, which is the task entrusted to him.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {ولن أجد من دونه ملتحدا}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatada says God selects an approved messenger, shows him what He wills of the unseen, and chooses him for that disclosure.
rows.anchor: بلاغا من الله ورسالاته وفي قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God informs messengers of unseen matters by revelation, revealing what He wills; none but God knows His own decision.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the guards sent before and behind the messenger as angels who protect him from Satan until he conveys the message.

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies the approved messenger as Gabriel.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says each revealed verse came with four angels who guarded it until it reached the Prophet, ensuring the messengers delivered God's messages.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report relayed by Ibn Jurayj says poor believers enter Paradise forty years before rich believers, who are questioned about their worldly power and gifts.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج في قوله: {وذرني والمكذبين أولي النعمة} قال: بلغنا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj interprets the instruction to give the deniers a little respite as lasting until the sword.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God has a reckoning and purpose concerning the affluent deniers, and glosses ankāl as shackles.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {وذرني والمكذبين أولي النعمة ومهلهم قليلا}

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود، مجاهد، عكرمة، حماد، طاووس
rows.claim: Ibn Masud, Mujahid, Ikrima, Hammad, and Tawus all gloss ankāl as shackles or chains.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد عن ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan specifies that the chains are made of fire.

rows.speaker: سليمان التيمي
rows.claim: Sulayman al-Taymi says the chains are heavy and will never be undone, and he wept.
rows.anchor: عبد الرزاق وعبد بن حميد عن سليمان التيمي

rows.speaker: أبو عمران الجوني
rows.claim: Abu Imran al-Jawni says the chains will never be released from the condemned.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the choking food as thorny, caught in the throat, unable to go in or come out.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas identifies the choking food as the tree of Zaqqum; Mujahid gives the same view.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Humran reports that the Prophet recited the passage about chains, fire, choking food, and painful punishment, then fainted at the final word.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A separate report says the Prophet heard a man reciting about chains and blazing fire and fainted.
rows.anchor: من طريق حمران بن أعين أبي حرب بن أبي الأسود أن النبي

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid identifies the great warning as Hell.

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abu Razin says the warning to humankind is Hell.
rows.anchor: عن أبي رزين {إنها لإحدى الكبر نذيرا للبشر}

rows.speaker: حذيفة
rows.claim: Hudhayfa says a caller warns each morning and evening that people must depart; he links this warning to the Quran's call to advance or fall behind.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses advancing as following obedience to God and falling behind as lagging in it.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس {لمن شاء منكم أن يتقدم أو يتأخر}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says advancing means obedience and falling behind means disobedience.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة {لمن شاء منكم أن يتقدم}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says each soul is held accountable for what it earned.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says all people are held by their deeds except the people of the right.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة {كل نفس بما كسبت رهينة إلا أصحاب اليمين}

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the people of the right will not be subjected to reckoning.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد في قوله: {كل نفس بما كسبت رهينة إلا أصحاب اليمين}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the people of the right as Muslims.

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali identifies the people of the right as Muslim children; Ibn Umar reports the same view.
rows.anchor: عن علي بن أبي طالب في قوله

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn Zubayr's recitation inserts a direct address, reading that people in gardens ask the criminals, O so-and-so, what brought you to Saqar; Umar is also reported to have read it so.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: One report from Ibn Abbas says Surat al-Insan was revealed in Mecca.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr says Surat Hal Ata was revealed in Mecca.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas places the revelation of Surat al-Insan in Medina, differing from the Meccan reports.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports an Ethiopian man asking whether faith and matching the Prophet's deeds would bring him to Paradise; the Prophet affirmed, promised divine reward, and the man died longing for the promised vision.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A trusted-source report says a black man asked often about praise of God; when the Prophet recited the Paradise description in this surah, the man sighed and died of longing for Paradise.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd tells of a black man who died after sighing at the surah's description of Paradise; the Prophet said longing for Paradise had taken his soul.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Al-Hakim authenticates Abu Dharr's report that, after reciting the surah, the Prophet described the heavens creaking with angels, each space of four fingers containing a prostrating angel; knowing this would make people weep and abandon worldly pleasure.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the human being had a period of existence before creation.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {هل أتى على الإنسان حين من الدهر}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says humanity was created recently, and no creature came after humankind.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {هل أتى على الإنسان حين من الدهر} قال: الإنسان أتى عليه حين من الدهر {لم يكن شيئا مذكورا} قال

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: When Umar heard the verse, he wished that it were complete.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud likewise wished the verse were complete, then picked up a twig and said he wished he were like it.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says Adam was the last of creation.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {هل أتى على الإنسان حين من الدهر} قال: إن آدم آخر ما خلق من الخلق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-insan means every human being.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says there are periods no one can know; no one knows how long passed before God created the human being.

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: After reciting the verse, Umar exclaims that God made the human being hearing, seeing, alive, and dead.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud connects the Quran with embryonic stages: after forty days each as a drop and clot, an angel writes sex, destiny, provision, effects, and term; he glosses amshaj as the embryo's veins.

rows.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
rows.claim: An unattributed poem describes black clouds whose water is thajjāj, providing poetic evidence for abundant, pouring rain.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-muʿṣirāt are winds and thajjāj is pouring water.
rows.anchor: والخرائطي من طرق عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud describes clouds carrying water and raining it like a full udder, in heavy showers distributed by winds.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies al-muʿṣirāt as clouds and thajjāj as pouring or abundant.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد وابن جرير عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas says al-muʿṣirāt means from heaven and thajjāj means pouring.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر عن الربيع بن أنس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: The report notes the wording in Fadl ibn Abbas's codex for the rain verse.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reports Ibn Abbas's reading identifying the source as winds.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في مصحف الفضل بن عباس

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says al-muʿṣirāt are winds, reads bi-l-muʿṣirāt, and glosses thajjāj as pouring.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the gardens are clustered together.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the gardens are intertwined.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the gardens are interwoven with one another.
rows.anchor: عبد الرزاق وعبد بن حميد وابن جرير عن قتادة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says crops become gardens when their parts grow close together.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر عن عكرمة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also describes gardens whose parts have grown intertwined.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the Day of Decision is an appointed time, when God magnifies the day and judges the earlier and later peoples.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد وابن جرير وابن المنذر عن قتادة

rows.speaker: إبراهيم النخعي
rows.claim: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i says the earth was spread out from Mecca.
rows.anchor: أخرج ابن المنذر عن إبراهيم النخعي

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj glosses the water as rivers made to flow and pasture as all the plants and other growth God created.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says spreading the earth brought out its water and pasture, opened rivers, and placed mountains, sands, roads, and hills across it in two days.
rows.anchor: ابن بي حاتم عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the provision for people as benefit.

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: Ata says he heard that the earth was spread from beneath the Kaaba.

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali reports the Prophet praising God as the one who spread and created the earth.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-tammah al-kubra is one of the names of the Resurrection Day.

rows.speaker: القاسم بن الوليد الهمذاني
rows.claim: Al-Qasim ibn al-Walid says the great calamity is when the people of Paradise are driven to Paradise and the people of Hell to Hell.
rows.anchor: عن القاسم بن الوليد الهمذاني في قوله

rows.speaker: عمرو بن قيس الكندي
rows.claim: Amr ibn Qays says it is when the command comes to take someone to the Fire.

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says Hell will be exposed to whoever looks.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the great calamity is when people are sent to Malik, guardian of Hell; ṭaghā means disobeyed, marsāhā means its time, and its mention means the Hour.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد رضي الله عنه في قوله: {فإذا جاءت الطامة}

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali says people asked the Prophet about the Hour, then the verse asked what he had to do with its mention.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A weakly transmitted report says Meccan polytheists mockingly asked when the Hour would come; its timing belongs to God, Muhammad warns those who fear it, and the world will seem only an evening or morning.

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha says the Prophet was repeatedly asked about the Hour until these verses were revealed, after which he stopped asking about it.

rows.speaker: عروة
rows.claim: A mursal report from Urwah gives the same account that the Prophet stopped asking about the Hour after these verses.
rows.anchor: وأخرجه سعيد بن منصور وابن المنذر وابن أبي حاتم وابن مردويه عن عروة مرسلا

rows.speaker: طارق بن شهاب
rows.claim: Tariq ibn Shihab says the Prophet often mentioned the Hour, then stopped after these verses were revealed.

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that when visiting Bedouins asked about the Hour, the Prophet pointed to the youngest person and said that if he lived a century, their own Hour would have come.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says Paradise is entered by one who hopes for it, Hell is avoided by one who fears it, and God shows mercy to one who is merciful.

rows.speaker: ابن جرير
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj glosses the Hour's endpoint as God's knowledge and interprets the brief evening and morning as worldly time.
rows.anchor: ابن المنذر عن ابن جرير في قوله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says worldly life will seem slight to people when they see the affair of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة في قوله: {كأنهم يوم يرونها}

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the night turns away and the morning breathes when daylight begins at dawn.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says ʿasʿasa can mean the night arriving or departing.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas tells Nafi ibn al-Azraq that ʿasʿasa means the onset of darkness and cites al-Nabigha's poetry as evidence.

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali came out at dawn, called it a good time for the witr prayer, and recited the oath by night and breathing morning.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the noble messenger as Gabriel.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس إن نافع بن الأزرق

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada identifies the noble messenger as Gabriel and says the clear horizon is where daylight comes from or where the sun rises.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر عن قتادة

rows.speaker: جبريل
rows.claim: Gabriel tells the Prophet that his strength lifted the four cities of Lot, each with four hundred thousand fighters, until heaven heard their animals; he destroyed them and faithfully did only what he was commanded.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: During the Night Journey, the Prophet asked Gabriel to reveal Hell; the report explains Gabriel's being obeyed and trusted with revelation and says Muhammad is not mad.
rows.anchor: ابن المنذر عن ابن عباس قال:

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says Gabriel is trusted with seventy veils and enters them without permission; the Prophet is the companion declared not mad.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr say Surat al-Fajr was revealed in Mecca; the section also classifies the surah as Meccan and thirty verses.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet rebuked Muadh for overlong prayer and directed him to recite shorter chapters, including the chapters beginning with glorification, the sun, dawn, and night.

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr says God swears by the dawn.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن الزبير في قوله

rows.speaker: ميمون بن مهران
rows.claim: Maymun ibn Mihran says God may swear by any of His creation, while no one may swear except by God.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas interprets the dawn as daybreak.

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima identifies the dawn as morning, and elsewhere as dawn at Muzdalifa on the morning of the gathering.
rows.anchor: عبد بن حميد عن عكرمة في قوله:

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the dawn is specifically that of the Sacrifice Day, not every dawn; Muhammad ibn Ka'b agrees.
rows.anchor: ابن أبي حاتم عن مجاهد في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the dawn as the dawn prayer.
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن جرير عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the dawn as Muharram, the first dawn of the year.

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says the best fasting after Ramadan is in God's month of Muharram, and the best prayer after the obligatory prayer is night prayer.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: أفضل الصيام

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: Ali tells a man asking which month to fast after Ramadan to fast Muharram, God's month, which includes the day God accepted one people's repentance and forgave others.
